561.quote_or_event: “The Lord and Master is True, and True is His justice. He issues His Commands according to His judgement.”
561.explanation: Closing his hymn on Babar's invasion, Guru Nanak affirms that the Lord's commands follow from true judgement, so that what befalls each person answers to justice.
561.tie_back: The Kural says a true king first inquires fairly and then punishes in due measure; Guru Nanak's model of justice is likewise a command that issues only from true judgement.
561.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
561._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse speaks of divine justice, not of a human ruler's procedure of inquiry and proportionate punishment.

562.quote_or_event: “Your child makes mistakes again and again, but still, You are pleased with him, O Father of the Universe.”
562.explanation: Guru Ram Das pictures God as a father who goes on loving his child in spite of repeated faults.
562.tie_back: The Kural advises raising the rod sternly but letting it fall gently; Guru Ram Das gives the ideal of a guardian whose correction is always tempered by tender regard.
562.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1321, Raag Kalyaan, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
562._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the verse is about divine forgiveness of the devotee, not a ruler's measured punishment, and it has nothing like the Kural's stern warning.

563.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, to use force is tyranny, even if you call it legal.”
563.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose verses the Gurus placed in the scripture, rejects the excuse that violence becomes acceptable once it is given a lawful name.
563.tie_back: The Kural says the cruel-sceptred king whose habit is to spread dread will surely and swiftly be ruined; Kabir insists that force remains tyranny whatever legal dress it wears.
563.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
563._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Kabir's immediate context is ritual slaughter of animals called halal, so the application to a ruler's terror is an extension, and the verse does not speak of the tyrant's ruin.

564.quote_or_event: “Gathering the wealth of Maya, you earn an evil reputation.”
564.explanation: Guru Arjan warns the one who heaps up wealth by pressing on others that what he really earns is the ill name and ill wishes of the people.
564.tie_back: The Kural says a king whom his subjects call ‘cruel’ will have his span cut short; Guru Arjan likewise notes that oppressive gain earns the people's bitter verdict.
564.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 42, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
564._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the people's ill verdict on the oppressor is shared, but the verse addresses any grasping person rather than a king, and does not predict a shortened reign.

565.quote_or_event: Guru Amar Das made it a rule that anyone who wished to see him had first to eat in the casteless langar, sitting with everyone else, and it was said that even the Mughal emperor Akbar ate there and sought his advice.
565.explanation: The Guru's presence was open to all comers on equal terms, through a shared meal rather than through rank or favour.
565.tie_back: The Kural says the wealth of a ruler who is hard to see and harsh of face is like treasure guarded by a demon; the Sikh tradition made access to the Guru open and equal for every visitor, ruler and commoner alike.
565._accuracy_note: Next-best: the open, equal access fits, but the langar rule is about equality rather than a ruler's pleasant face, and Britannica reports the Akbar episode only as something that ‘was said’.

566.quote_or_event: “who speaks insipid words with his tongue, is ruined, again and again.”
566.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that the person whose tongue utters harsh, graceless (phikka) words brings ruin on himself again and again.
566.tie_back: The Kural says the vast wealth of a ruler who is harsh in speech and lacks kindly regard will not last; Guru Amar Das likewise ties harsh speech to repeated ruin.
566.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 594, Raag Vadhans, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
566._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on harsh speech leading to ruin; the ruin meant is chiefly spiritual, and the verse says nothing of wealth or kingship (Sant Singh Khalsa's ‘insipid’ renders phikka, which also means rude or harsh).

567.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid.”
567.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that harsh, graceless speech gradually drains the speaker himself, body and mind.
567.tie_back: The Kural says harsh words and excessive punishment are a file that slowly wears away a king's strength; Guru Nanak likewise sees harsh speech as wearing down the one who uses it.
567.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
567._accuracy_note: Next-best: the self-erosion caused by harsh words matches, but the verse is about the inner life, not about punishment or a ruler's power over enemies.

568.quote_or_event: “Tatta: In anger, you are burnt, you fool. T'hat'ha: That place where you live, is cursed.”
568.explanation: In his acrostic Patti, Guru Amar Das warns the learned man that anger burns him up and spoils the very place where he dwells.
568.tie_back: The Kural says a king who acts without deliberating with his counsellors and lashes out in anger will see his fortune shrink; Guru Amar Das likewise shows anger consuming the angry man and his surroundings.
568.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 435, Raag Aasaa (Patti), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
568._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the destructiveness of anger is shared, but the verse has nothing on failing to consult counsellors, which is half of the Kural's point.

569.quote_or_event: “Millions of religious leaders failed to halt the invader, when they heard of the Emperor's invasion.”
569.explanation: Guru Nanak records that when Babar's invasion was announced, the Lodi rulers relied on the prayers and charms of holy men instead of real defence, and none of it stopped the invader.
569.tie_back: The Kural says a king who has not prepared his defences beforehand will be seized with fear when war comes and quickly perish; Guru Nanak describes rulers caught unready and falling in just this way.
569.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
569._accuracy_note: Strong fit on rulers unprepared when war arrived; the reading that the Lodis trusted charms instead of defence follows the standard commentary rather than the bare line itself.

570.quote_or_event: “Deer, falcons and government officials are known to be trained and clever. When the trap is set, they trap their own kind; hereafter they will find no place of rest.”
570.explanation: Guru Nanak compares the officials of an oppressive state to decoy deer and hunting falcons, trained creatures used to snare their own kind.
570.tie_back: The Kural says the heaviest burden on the earth is a harsh sceptre that binds unlearned men to itself as its helpers; Guru Nanak shows how such rule works through trained servants who prey on their own people.
570.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar (Malaar ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
570._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on tyranny working through compliant servants, though Guru Nanak calls them ‘trained and clever’ rather than unlearned, and stresses their own fate rather than the earth's burden.
